transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Start: 15:00 PDT
Scheduled duration: 60 min (actual 58)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Esha Rao (Redwood SE); Jon Patel (Redwood Solutions); Carlos Vega (Sirius VP Eng); Priya Anand (SRE Lead); Dr. Samir Rao (ML Infra); Elena Morales (Product)

Summary (auto): quick deep dive on p95/p99 tail causes observed in Sirius staging — suspecting KV-cache hotkeys + cross-AZ network hops; discuss streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs and quantization ops for inference. Agree to run targeted benchmarks in Sirius dev VPC and share topology.

Topics: KV cache behavior, hotkey distributions, batching strategies, streaming vs non-streaming tail effects, network hop tracing, on-prem/VPC considerations, quantization impact.

Action items recap (at end of call also): see action_items metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to do a focused troubleshooting session around the p95/p99 spikes you reported in staging, right?
[00:30] Carlos Vega: Yeah thanks Maya. We're seeing intermittent high tails in both streaming and non-streaming endpoints. It's very bursty, usually during morning syncs. P95 is fine but p99 blows up to like 1.8s from a 220ms baseline.
[01:05] Esha Rao: Got it. Can you confirm whether those calls are hitting the same model version and whether there's any routing fallback enabled?
[01:25] Carlos Vega: It's the same model pinned to v2.4. No explicit fallback configured — we do have a staged canary but not active right now.
[01:40] Priya Anand: One callout — some of our clients are routed through an on-prem proxy that does TLS termination; that might add hops. We recently changed the peering and added a new transit in us-west-2b.
[02:05] Jon Patel: That could be it. Network hops + cold KV entries are classic tail latency comp combo. We'll try to unpack both.
[02:25] Dr. Samir Rao: Quick background: our workload is conversational summarization for device logs. We have a strong hotkey distribution — about 10% of prefixes account for ~60% of traffic.
[02:50] Esha Rao: Perfect, that's exactly the hotkey scenario where prefix/KV cache gets overwhelmed causing tailing, especially when combined with batching and cache misses. Two immediate axes: KV cache hit rate and network hop variability.
[03:20] Elena Morales: Also curious about streaming — some of our product team says streaming seems worse, but it's not clear whether streaming client-side buffering or server-side append is to blame.
[03:45] Maya Chen: We'll run streaming vs non-streaming head-to-head in a controlled benchmark. Esha, can you outline the experimental plan?
[04:00] Esha Rao: Sure. Step 1: replay a 1-hour trace of real traffic against a dedicated dev cluster. We'll test three scenarios: (A) streaming on with small chunk sizes, (B) non-streaming single response, (C) streaming but with aggressive prefix caching (larger KV reservations). We'll instrument per-request latencies and per-token.
[04:35] Carlos Vega: For hardware, we can give you 2x A10G nodes in dev for a day. Would that be enough?
[04:50] Jon Patel: For initial KV hotkey profiling, yes. If we need to push throughput, we might want 4 GPUs. We'll start small.
[05:05] Priya Anand: I'll flag that we run across two AZs and there's NAT and transit gateways in between — I'll send the diagram.
[05:20] Maya Chen: Thanks, Priya. One nuance: streaming can exacerbate p99 because of tail variance in per-token kernel launches + network ack patterns. Also, if KV cache population is happening mid-stream you get a compounded delay.
[05:50] Carlos Vega: So is the answer smarter batching or more aggressive caching?
[06:05] Esha Rao: Both. There's no silver bullet but three levers: 1) adaptive batching (smaller target latency with dynamic batch cutoff), 2) prefix hotkey replication — we can replicate top-K prefixes to local nodes, and 3) quantization to reduce kernel latencies (int8 sometimes helps, int4 can hurt for some ops depending on kernel availability).
[06:40] Dr. Samir Rao: Replication sounds heavy. How does Redwood handle KV replication across GPUs/instances?
[06:55] Jon Patel: We do a tiered approach: local in-memory L1 for hot prefixes (per-host), fallback L2 distributed KV with async replication. For private deployments we can pin hot keys to dedicated instances to reduce cross-host hops.
[07:25] Priya Anand: If we pin keys to instances, that could be a single point of failure unless we do leader election.
[07:40] Esha Rao: Right — we keep an async replicate pipeline so reads are local-most of the time, and if a node fails, there's a brief failover. That introduces complexity but reduces tail latency.
[08:00] Carlos Vega: Can you quantify the latency improvements? Ballpark numbers.
[08:10] Esha Rao: In our internal tests with a 10% hotkey distribution, L1 local cache cut p99 by ~60-70% for those hot prefixes — overall endpoint p99 improved about 30-40% depending on workload.
[08:35] Carlos Vega: That's promising. What about network hops? We suspect the new transit gateway adds ~150ms sometimes.
[08:50] Jon Patel: We saw that cross-AZ extra hop can add tail variance. It's not constant — perf depends on transient queueing in routers. We'll need packet-level traces (tcpdump) or application traces (x-forwarded-for plus per-hop timestamps).
[09:15] Priya Anand: We can run perf traces but can't share raw pcap externally. Would Redwood accept sanitized traces?
[09:30] Maya Chen: Absolutely, sanitized is fine — we just need timing info and hop counts.
[09:40] Elena Morales: Quick question on quantization: our models are Llama-derivative. We're nervous about int4 giving hallucination or quality drift.
[09:55] Esha Rao: Totally fair. For Llama-family models, we recommend a staged quantization: int8 dynamic per-layer first, run evals; if quality holds, try int4 with per-channel calibration. Also Redwood Optimize suggests mixed-precision on a per-layer basis. We'll provide the eval harness.
[10:25] Carlos Vega: Does quantization affect streaming vs batching differently?
[10:35] Esha Rao: Quantization mostly affects kernel compute time and memory bandwidth — streaming still involves per-token kernel dispatch overhead. However with lower precision you can get faster kernel times which shrinks per-token tail. But if streaming overhead dominates (like network ACKs), then compute wins less.
[11:00] Priya Anand: On our side, we've instrumented and see two classes of p99: compute-bound (high seq len) and network-bound (short seq, high calls). Most of our spikes fall into network-bound.
[11:20] Jon Patel: For network-bound workloads, local caching + reducing inter-node calls helps more than quantization. But it's workload dependent.
[11:35] Maya Chen: Let's talk about methodology — how we'll measure p95/p99 consistently across streaming vs non-streaming.
[11:45] Esha Rao: We'll use a synchronous emitter that simulates clients: for streaming, we'll measure time-to-first-byte, time-to-last-byte, and per-token latencies; for non-streaming, we'll measure total request latency. We'll also capture server-side timestamps (enqueue, start_compute, end_compute, write_response).
[12:20] Carlos Vega: Can we add distributed tracing headers? We already propagate x-request-id.
[12:30] Maya Chen: Yes add those, and Redwood will honor and return the same id in logs so we can stitch traces.
[12:40] Priya Anand: Are there any recommended kernel/runtime flags we should try? We run NVIDIA drivers with Triton.
[12:55] Esha Rao: For Triton/Trition — a few notes: enable pinned memory and CUDA stream fusion where possible; set small kernel-preload for low-latency workloads; avoid large dynamic batching windows that increase latency. Also try our continuous batching mode which keeps batch window tiny but opportunistic.
[13:25] Carlos Vega: Continuous batching — is that in Redwood hosted only or available in private?
[13:35] Jon Patel: It's part of the runtime and can be enabled both in Dedicated and Private deployments; config differs a bit in networking knobs.
[13:50] Elena Morales: Back to KV hotkeys: Dr. Samir mentioned top-20 prefixes. What's the process to identify hotkeys quickly?
[14:05] Esha Rao: We ingest prefix metrics at the gateway for a 24h window and compute top-K. We then create a candidate set to pre-warm in L1 cache. We also sample tail latency per prefix to prioritize.
[14:30] Dr. Samir Rao: We can export those logs; Priya will sanitize and share later.
[14:40] Priya Anand: Yep I'll include that in the topology packet.
[14:45] Carlos Vega: A weird observation — some p99 spikes correlated with heavy egress to analytics pipelines. Could that be competing for NIC or host CPU?
[14:58] Esha Rao: Absolutely. Host contension (NIC queueing, CPU interrupts) can create tail spikes. On shared hosts, co-scheduled workloads matter. For Private, isolation helps; for Hosted, we do noisy-neighbor controls.
[15:20] Maya Chen: We'll check host-level metrics too. Please include NIC saturation counters; if possible, ethtool stats across the window.
[15:35] Priya Anand: We'll extract NIC counters.
[15:40] Jon Patel: Another mitigant is to preferentially schedule inference on dedicated NICs or use SR-IOV.
[15:50] Carlos Vega: On that note, on-prem options — if we move to an air-gapped setup, how do you handle KV replication and cluster coordination?
[16:05] Esha Rao: In air-gapped/on-prem, we do multi-zone replication over private fabric. We can ship a bundle that uses our control-plane relay or a customer-managed control plane. For security, we integrate with KMS/HSM for keys. Latency-wise, on-prem typically reduces network hops but requires careful topology to avoid a single fabric bottleneck.
[16:35] Elena Morales: Any gotchas with SSO/SAML or audit logs in private?
[16:45] Maya Chen: We integrate with SAML/SSO and can ship enhanced audit-log retention as an add-on. We'll share the SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[16:55] Carlos Vega: Cool. Can we walk through a quick root-cause simulation — you said pipeline: request -> gateway -> L1 -> L2 -> model compute. Walk me through where the 1.8s spike likely lives.
[17:12] Esha Rao: Sure. If it's network-bound: client -> transit gateway -> extra hop -> Redwood gateway -> node (remote L2 call) -> wait for remote L1 fetch -> compute start. The remote L2 fetch plus extra hop could easily add 500-800ms depending on queues. Then if compute is cold (KV miss) you get kernel startup cost, adding another 200-400ms. Combined you can get into the ~1.5-2s tail.
[17:55] Priya Anand: That maps to our observations.
[18:05] Carlos Vega: What telemetry would prove remote L2 fetch is happening?
[18:15] Jon Patel: Two signals: 1) hop-specific latency spikes in distributed trace timestamps, 2) elevated L2 fetch counts with matching timestamps in server logs.
[18:30] Dr. Samir Rao: We'll look for those.
[18:40] Maya Chen: Ok, any quick wins we can try before the benchmark?
[18:48] Esha Rao: Yes: 1) Pre-warm top-20 prefixes on a small subset of nodes (fastest change), 2) reduce the batching window for streaming clients to lower tail variability, 3) pin latency-sensitive routes to Dedicated capacity if available.
[19:08] Carlos Vega: Pre-warm — how long does that take?
[19:15] Esha Rao: A few minutes to populate L1, depends on volume. We'll provide a script to stream warmup traffic.
[19:25] Priya Anand: We'll try pre-warm tonight in staging.
[19:30] Maya Chen: Great. Switching gear — tracing noise: our logs sometimes show speaker labels like "Speaker 2" in transcripts. Not relevant but if you see weird transcript names in the exported logs, ignore.
[19:45] (laughter)
[19:50] Carlos Vega: Haha noted.
[20:00] Esha Rao: I'd like to propose a benchmark matrix: axis 1 = streaming/non-streaming; axis 2 = caching config (no cache / L2-only / L1 local); axis 3 = quantization (fp16 / int8 / int4). We'll run each cell for 10-15 minutes with realistic arrival patterns.
[20:30] Maya Chen: That sounds perfect. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and token-level latencies. Also capture tail composition: network vs compute breakdown.
[20:45] Priya Anand: For the arrival pattern — we can replay real traces but mask PII.
[20:55] Carlos Vega: Yes we'll sanitize.
[21:05] Dr. Samir Rao: A note on int4 — for some layers we've seen small output distribution shifts; need MML evals to ensure quality.
[21:20] Esha Rao: We'll run eval harness and diff. Redwood Optimize can flag regressions against your golden prompts.
[21:30] Jon Patel: Regarding network hops — can you give us traceroutes for the spike windows? Even just per-request ping timestamps helps.
[21:45] Priya Anand: We'll collect tracert and TCP RTTs for a 24h window and send.
[21:55] Maya Chen: Thanks. Any questions on resource limits, like kernel concurrency or KV memory sizing?
[22:05] Carlos Vega: How much memory should we allocate for KV L1 if we hot-replicate top-20 prefixes?
[22:15] Esha Rao: Depends on prefix size. If each prefix state is ~600KB average and top-20 equals ~12MB — trivial. But for conversation-level KV that stores longer histories, plan for 1-2GB. We'll help estimate once we see sample sizes.
[22:40] Priya Anand: We don't store whole conversation in KV, just prefix embeddings ~8-16KB. So numbers will be modest.
[22:50] Esha Rao: Great, L1 will be cheap then.
[23:00] Carlos Vega: Anything else on batching? We saw that larger batches reduce cost but increase p95. Is there an automated strategy?
[23:10] Jon Patel: We have adaptive batching that targets a latency SLO. It uses an exponential backoff on batch windows based on recent latencies. For workloads that need consistent p99, set the SLO tighter.
[23:35] Dr. Samir Rao: Are these settings per-route? We have multiple routes for low-latency telemetry vs heavy summarization.
[23:45] Maya Chen: Yes per-route configs in the console — you can dial SLOs per endpoint.
[23:55] Priya Anand: Good.
[24:05] Esha Rao: One more complexity: streaming with chunked responses means the server will do more frequent writes. If your network has higher packet loss or retransmits, that manifests as tail jitter. For that, you want fewer, larger chunks or better TCP tuning.
[24:30] Carlos Vega: We'll have our infra team look at MTU and retransmits.
[24:40] Maya Chen: Okay we're at half hour — want to do a quick live demo of how our traces look?
[24:50] Esha Rao: Sure, I'll share my screen and walk through a sample trace from our lab.
[25:00] (screen share started)
[25:05] Esha Rao: Here's a distributed trace showing enqueue, remote L2 fetch, and compute. Notice the L2 fetch spike at 320ms. You can see the per-hop annotations.
[25:25] Carlos Vega: That remote fetch is exactly what we think is happening.
[25:35] Esha Rao: On the right panel is the heatmap for per-prefix tail latencies — you can spot hotkeys.
[25:50] Priya Anand: Helpful. How do we get that UI output? Is that in the Redwood console?
[26:00] Jon Patel: Yes it's available in the Console for Dedicated and Hosted; for Private we can ship the observability agent to produce similar outputs.
[26:15] Dr. Samir Rao: For the benchmark, will you push the agent to our dev VPC?
[26:25] Maya Chen: We'll provide an agent package and deployment instructions.
[26:35] Elena Morales: Regarding pricing for Dedicated to pin routes — can you give a rough estimate?
[26:45] Maya Chen: We'll send formal pricing, but rough guidance: a small Dedicated pool (4 GPU-equivalent) starts at mid-five figures per month. I'll follow up in email.
[27:05] Carlos Vega: Ok. Back to traces — any suggestions for sampling rate so we capture p99 without too much overhead?
[27:20] Esha Rao: Capture 100% of request timestamps but sample full payloads at 1-5% and always capture headers with IDs so we can reconstruct.
[27:35] Priya Anand: That should be doable.
[27:40] Carlos Vega: Any red flags in your logs we should watch for right away?
[27:50] Jon Patel: Watch for bursts of L2 fetches coincident with increased queuing on gateways; also look for GC/pause events if you're on JVMs upstream.
[28:05] Dr. Samir Rao: We're mostly Go so GC less likely but we'll still check.
[28:15] Maya Chen: Two quick clarifying Qs: 1) Is the staging traffic representative? 2) Do you have perf counters for host NIC and CPU?
[28:25] Carlos Vega: Staging is close, not perfect. We'll provide a production trace sample with masked PII. And yes we can expose NIC counters.
[28:40] Esha Rao: Great.
[28:45] (5-minute cross talk while sharing links)
[33:50] Maya Chen: Alright — resume. One operational note: if you go with prefix replication, you should monitor eviction rates; evictions at L1 cause sudden cascades to L2 and likely tail spikes.
[34:10] Priya Anand: How do you recommend eviction policy? LRU? TTL-based?
[34:20] Esha Rao: A hybrid policy — weighted LRU with TTL for stale prefixes works well. For hotkeys prefer pinning rather than pure caching.
[34:35] Carlos Vega: Pinning cost vs benefit — we'll model it.
[34:45] Jon Patel: Also consider multi-zone awareness: pin hotkeys to nodes in each AZ to avoid cross-AZ fetches.
[34:55] Dr. Samir Rao: That requires more memory but saves tail.
[35:05] Maya Chen: Quick check on instrumentation: include time-to-first-byte for streaming clients in the trace; often that tells you if network or compute dominated.
[35:20] Priya Anand: Will do.
[35:25] Elena Morales: Any thoughts on headroom — how much extra capacity should we reserve to avoid hitting tails under load?
[35:35] Esha Rao: For typical conversational workloads, 20-30% headroom gives solid buffer. For bursty telemetry, consider burst capacity or autoscaling policies with very short cooldowns.
[35:55] Carlos Vega: Do you support pre-warmed burst pools?
[36:05] Jon Patel: Yes Dedicated supports burstable capacity with instant cold-start policies; Private requires pre-provisioning but we have scripts to automate scale-up.
[36:20] Priya Anand: One final question on metrics: do you expose kernel-level per-token times?
[36:30] Esha Rao: We expose a compute breakdown that includes kernel dispatch, KV fetch time, and serialization time per token when instrumentation is enabled.
[36:45] Carlos Vega: Great.
[36:50] Maya Chen: We're approaching the end — let's summarize next steps.
[36:55] Esha Rao: Action list: Redwood will run benchmark in dev VPC (Maya/Esha/Jon). Sirius will send topology, hotkey list, and traces (Carlos/Priya/Dr. Samir). We'll run the benchmark and share results by 2025-07-29. We'll also send quantization evaluation harness.
[37:20] Carlos Vega: Sounds good.
[37:25] Priya Anand: One date correction — we can send the topology by 07/25, hotkeys by 07/24.
[37:35] Maya Chen: Perfect.
[37:40] Elena Morales: Any blockers for the pilot?
[37:45] Jon Patel: Just access to the dev VPC and the two A10G nodes — once we have that, we can start.
[37:55] Carlos Vega: We'll provision and share creds via secure channel.
[38:05] Maya Chen: Great. Any final Qs?
[38:10] (brief silence)
[38:15] Dr. Samir Rao: No further questions. Appreciate the practical steps.
[38:20] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll email the test plan and links.
[38:25] Carlos Vega: Thank you.
[38:30] (call ends)

Post-call notes (auto): Redwood to deliver benchmark config, pre-warm scripts, quantization checklist, and sample console traces. Sirius to share topology, hotkey list, and sanitized traces. Follow-up scheduled if needed after benchmark results.
